Content:
When solving ODEs numerically:

Content:
- The solution is advanced in many steps.
- Each step introduces a small error (LTE).
- These errors propagate forward (contributing to GTE).

Content:
Stability describes how a numerical method responds to these small perturbations.

Content:
A method is stable if small errors remain controlled as the computation proceeds.
A method is unstable if small errors can grow rapidly, even when the true solution stays well-behaved.

Content:
Stability determines how local errors turn into global errors: a method may be accurate in a single step, but if it is unstable, the global error can grow without bound.

Content:
One way to study stability is to test a numerical method on the following test equation:

Content:
[MATH: y' = -\lambda y, \qquad y(0)=1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad \lambda > 0]

Content:
The exact solution of the test equation is [MATH: y(x) = e^{-\lambda x},] which satisfies [MATH: y(x) \to 0] as [MATH: x \to \infty.]

Content:
We say that a numerical method with update formula [MATH: y_{n+1} = y_n + \Delta y] is stable for a given step size [MATH: \Delta x] if, when applied to the test equation, the numerical solution also satisfies

Content:
[MATH: y_n \to 0 \:\text{ as }\: n \to \infty.]

Content:
To see how this works in practice, let's analyze the stability of Euler's method.

items.readable_text:
Content:
We will now check the stability of Euler's method by applying it to the test equation

Content:
[MATH: y' = -\lambda y, \qquad y(0)=1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad \lambda > 0.]

Content:
First, recall that, for an initial value problem [MATH: y' = f(x,y), y(x_0) = y_0,] Euler's method is given by the update formula

Content:
[MATH: y_{n+1} = y_n + f(x_n, y_n) \cdot \Delta x.]

Content:
Applying Euler's method to the test equation, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: y_{n + 1}|= y_{n} + (− λy_{n}) ⋅ Δx; = y_{n} − λy_{n} ⋅ Δx; = (1 − λΔx)y_{n}]

Content:
Now, for stability, we require [MATH: y_n \to 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] Here, since [MATH: y_0=1,] we have

Content:
[MATH: y_{n}|= (1 − λΔx)y_{n − 1}; = (1 − λΔx)((1 − λΔx)y_{n − 2}); = (1 − λΔx)^{2}y_{n − 2}; ⋮⋮; = (1 − λΔx)^{n}y_{0}; = (1 − λΔx)^{n}.]

Content:
Let's define [MATH: R(\lambda\Delta x) = 1 - \lambda\Delta x.] Then, [MATH: y_n] converges to [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty] if and only if [MATH: |R(\lambda\Delta x)| < 1.] The function [MATH: R(\lambda\Delta x)] is called the stability function of Euler's method.

Content:
Expanding this inequality, we get

Content:
[MATH: |R(λΔx)||< 1;|1 − λΔx||< 1; − 1 < 1 − λΔx|< 1; − 2 < − λΔx|< 0; 0 < λΔx|< 2.]

Content:
This means that Euler's method is stable when applied to the test equation for values in the region [MATH: 0 < \lambda\Delta x < 2.]

Content:
The diagram below shows the exact solution curve with the numerical steps of Euler's method for the cases [MATH: \lambda\Delta x < 2] and [MATH: \lambda\Delta x = 2,] with [MATH: \lambda > 0] fixed.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f723b0574e30e665499be59c3e6e5136]

Content:
Notice that, for [MATH: \lambda\Delta x < 2,] the numerical values converge to [MATH: 0] (stable), whereas for [MATH: \lambda\Delta x = 2,] the values oscillate between [MATH: -1] and [MATH: 1] and do not converge to [MATH: 0] (unstable).

Content:
For values [MATH: \lambda\Delta x > 2,] the numerical solution would grow in magnitude at each step, leading to rapidly diverging values.

Now, let's check the stability of Euler's Method by applying it to the test equation [MATH: y' = -6y, \qquad y(0) = 8.]

First, for an initial value problem [MATH: y' = f(x,y), y(x_0) = y_0,] Euler's method is given by the update formula [MATH: y_{n+1} = y_n + f(x_n,y_n) \cdot \Delta x.]

Now, let's check our statements:

  • Applying Euler's method to the test equation, we get the following: [MATH: y_{n + 1}|= y_{n} + (− 6y_{n}) ⋅ Δx; = y_{n} − 6y_{n} ⋅ Δx; = (1 − 6Δx)y_{n}.] Hence, statement I is false.

  • For stability, we require [MATH: y_n \to 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] Here, we have [MATH: y_{n}|= (1 − 6Δx)y_{n − 1}; = (1 − 6Δx)((1 − 6Δx)y_{n − 2}); = (1 − 6Δx)^{2}y_{n − 2}; ⋮⋮; = (1 − 6Δx)^{n}y_{0}; = 8(1 − 6Δx)^{n}.] Therefore, [MATH: y_n] converges to [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty] if and only if [MATH: \left|1 - 6\Delta x\right| < 1,] as stated. Hence, statement II is true.

  • Expanding the inequality [MATH: \left|1 - 6\Delta x\right| < 1,] we get [MATH: − 1|< 1 − 6Δx < 1; − 2|< − 6Δx < 0; 0|< 6Δx < 2; 0|< Δx < (1)/(3).] Finally, we determine stability for the given step sizes:

    • Since [MATH: \Delta x = 0.1] satisfies the above inequality, Euler's method is stable for this value. Hence, statement III is true.

    • Since [MATH: \Delta x = 0.2] also satisfies the above inequality, Euler's method is stable for this value. Hence, statement IV is false.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II and III only".

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When solving ODEs numerically:

Content:
- The solution is advanced in many steps.
- Each step introduces a small error (LTE).
- These errors propagate forward (contributing to GTE).

Content:
Stability describes how a numerical method responds to these small perturbations.

Content:
A method is stable if small errors remain controlled as the computation proceeds.
A method is unstable if small errors can grow rapidly, even when the true solution stays well-behaved.

Content:
Stability determines how local errors turn into global errors: a method may be accurate in a single step, but if it is unstable, the global error can grow without bound.

Content:
One way to study stability is to test a numerical method on the following test equation:

Content:
[MATH: y' = -\lambda y, \qquad y(0)=1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad \lambda > 0]

Content:
The exact solution of the test equation is [MATH: y(x) = e^{-\lambda x},] which satisfies [MATH: y(x) \to 0] as [MATH: x \to \infty.]

Content:
We say that a numerical method with update formula [MATH: y_{n+1} = y_n + \Delta y] is stable for a given step size [MATH: \Delta x] if, when applied to the test equation, the numerical solution also satisfies

Content:
[MATH: y_n \to 0 \:\text{ as }\: n \to \infty.]

Content:
To see how this works in practice, let's analyze the stability of Euler's method.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Stability of Euler's Method

Content:
We will now check the stability of Euler's method by applying it to the test equation

Content:
[MATH: y' = -\lambda y, \qquad y(0)=1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad \lambda > 0.]

Content:
First, recall that, for an initial value problem [MATH: y' = f(x,y), y(x_0) = y_0,] Euler's method is given by the update formula

Content:
[MATH: y_{n+1} = y_n + f(x_n, y_n) \cdot \Delta x.]

Content:
Applying Euler's method to the test equation, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: y_{n + 1}|= y_{n} + (− λy_{n}) ⋅ Δx; = y_{n} − λy_{n} ⋅ Δx; = (1 − λΔx)y_{n}]

Content:
Now, for stability, we require [MATH: y_n \to 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] Here, since [MATH: y_0=1,] we have

Content:
[MATH: y_{n}|= (1 − λΔx)y_{n − 1}; = (1 − λΔx)((1 − λΔx)y_{n − 2}); = (1 − λΔx)^{2}y_{n − 2}; ⋮⋮; = (1 − λΔx)^{n}y_{0}; = (1 − λΔx)^{n}.]

Content:
Let's define [MATH: R(\lambda\Delta x) = 1 - \lambda\Delta x.] Then, [MATH: y_n] converges to [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty] if and only if [MATH: |R(\lambda\Delta x)| < 1.] The function [MATH: R(\lambda\Delta x)] is called the stability function of Euler's method.

Content:
Expanding this inequality, we get

Content:
[MATH: |R(λΔx)||< 1;|1 − λΔx||< 1; − 1 < 1 − λΔx|< 1; − 2 < − λΔx|< 0; 0 < λΔx|< 2.]

Content:
This means that Euler's method is stable when applied to the test equation for values in the region [MATH: 0 < \lambda\Delta x < 2.]

Content:
The diagram below shows the exact solution curve with the numerical steps of Euler's method for the cases [MATH: \lambda\Delta x < 2] and [MATH: \lambda\Delta x = 2,] with [MATH: \lambda > 0] fixed.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f723b0574e30e665499be59c3e6e5136]

Content:
Notice that, for [MATH: \lambda\Delta x < 2,] the numerical values converge to [MATH: 0] (stable), whereas for [MATH: \lambda\Delta x = 2,] the values oscillate between [MATH: -1] and [MATH: 1] and do not converge to [MATH: 0] (unstable).

Content:
For values [MATH: \lambda\Delta x > 2,] the numerical solution would grow in magnitude at each step, leading to rapidly diverging values.

Item 9 — Tutorial: Stability Functions, Stability Regions, and Absolute Stability

Content:
In general, when a numerical method
[MATH: y_{n+1} = y_n + \Delta y_n]
is applied to the test equation
[MATH: y' = -\lambda y, \qquad y(0) = 1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad \lambda > 0,]
we can write the update in the form
[MATH: y_{n+1} = R(\lambda\Delta x)y_n,]

As a geometric sequence, this decays to [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n\to\infty] if and only if [MATH: |R(\lambda\Delta x)| < 1.]

Content:
The set of values for which the method is stable, given by [MATH: |R(\lambda\Delta x)| < 1,] is called the stability region of the method.

Content:
A method that is stable for all possible values [MATH: \lambda\Delta x > 0] is called absolutely stable.

for all [MATH: \Delta x > 0.] So, the implicit Euler method is absolutely stable!
